A solo developer spent two months building an open source workspace called Cumora where your whole team shares AI agents inside group chats.

1/

Cumora solves a boring, expensive problem for small teams: turning engineers into human clipboards.

Right now, the smartest coding AIs like Claude Code and Codex live trapped inside one person's black terminal screen. Teammates cannot see what the AI is doing, so humans waste hours copying and pasting context between their terminal and Slack.

Cumora runs a small background program on your laptop that plugs your local AI straight into a shared group chat.

Most AI startups waste months trying to build their own agent brains from scratch using raw APIs.

Cumora skipped that trap entirely with a clever shortcut: instead of rebuilding file editors and terminal tools, it hijacks the command line tools that Anthropic and OpenAI already spent millions perfecting.

That changes the math for a small team in three core comparisons:

> Corporate API bills vs personal subscriptions
Instead of paying per word on a company API account, a team can share the flat $20 monthly subscriptions already logged in on their laptops.

> Private terminal vs shared room
Instead of one person gatekeeping the AI on their screen, the whole team sees the context and directs the same AI together.

> Deadlocked tasks vs automatic cover
When a teammate closes their laptop and their local AI goes offline, the remaining agents in the room automatically step in and take over the open tasks.

2/

Putting five independent AIs into one group chat usually creates a disaster where everyone replies at once or repeats the exact same answer.

Cumora built a referee server that filters every message on a strict step by step timeline:

> First 2.5 seconds: The system batches rapid messages together and wakes up a tiny, dirt cheap model first to decide if the expensive main model even needs to care.

> Right before replying: If Agent A posts an answer while Agent B is still thinking, the server blocks Agent B at the gate and forces it to read Agent A's new reply before speaking.

> At the database lock: If two agents try to save the exact same reply at the exact same millisecond, a database row lock kills the duplicate on the spot.

Where Cumora gets truly wild is how it handles team friction and autonomy. Instead of training bots to be polite yes men, it ships with four default profiles written to push back: a designer that rejects weak layouts, an engineer that refuses to code vague specs, and a product manager programmed to ask relentless follow up questions.

They also run on a 30 minute timer to check calendars and message people unprompted, spin up read only Whisper Rooms to debate technical plans before pitching humans, and keep a global trust score on every coworker that carries over across different projects.

3/

Giving autonomous agents access to your laptop and real email creates terrifying security edge cases. Because Cumora lets agents send and receive real emails, an early bug in the email router actually treated unverified outside email addresses as internal team members until an October patch fixed it.

Even riskier, out of the ten local AI engines Cumora supports, only Claude Code and Codex run inside a strict safety sandbox by default.

The other eight engines require turning the sandbox off, which hands a chat room AI full access to the files and keys on your computer.

Then comes the token furnace. Normally, AI providers save massive amounts of money by caching shared conversation history.

In Cumora, every agent puts its own private memory file, trust score, and read position at the very top of its prompt. Because every agent's instructions start differently, they cannot share cached data, meaning five agents in one room process the exact same group chat five separate times at full price.

One early tester put five agents in a room on a $20 monthly Claude plan and burned through the entire five hour quota in four chats, forcing an immediate upgrade to the $200 plan.

4/

This creates a brutal business paradox where everyone makes money off Cumora except Cumora. The app is completely free right now, and its killer feature is letting you bring your own laptop and existing AI subscriptions without paying Cumora a cent.

Meanwhile, because local agents go to sleep the moment you close your laptop, cloud hosts like exe dev stepped in to sell always on virtual machines preloaded with Cumora, while Anthropic and OpenAI pocket the $200 monthly subscription upgrades.

Cumora built the stage, and everyone else is collecting the ticket sales.

The ultimate plot twist is who built this and what happened next. Cumora was built almost single handedly by yetone, a top 0.05% GitHub developer who shipped 94 desktop updates in just two months.

One month after launching Cumora, he released a side tool called Magpie to solve the exact rate limit pain his users were hitting by pooling multiple AI accounts and switching models automatically when quotas run out. 

Cumora got 4,100 stars in two months, while Magpie exploded to 27,800 stars in 40 days.

Having five AI coworkers debate in a group chat is a fascinating vision of the future, but surviving the token bill is the urgent problem developers are stampeding to solve today.

❯ Networking: One ifconfig for Every Interface
Two ports bundled with LACP and a VLAN on top. On Ubuntu: 16 lines of YAML on disk and nine ip commands at the prompt, with a generator translating between them. On FreeBSD: four lines of rc.conf and two ifconfig commands, in the same words.
⠀
A server arrives with two network ports, and the switch team want them bundled with LACP and the machine reachable on VLAN 10. An ordinary Tuesday job, the sort of thing that should take ten minutes and occasionally takes the afternoon.
⠀
■ THE HABIT
⠀
On Ubuntu 26.04 the job starts in /etc/netplan, because the minimal installation pulls in netplan and iproute2 and leaves net-tools out, so ifconfig is not there unless someone asks for it. The file declares the two ports, a bond in mode 802.3ad and VLAN 10 with its address, sixteen lines once the indentation is right. Then netplan try applies it and rolls it back after 120 seconds unless you confirm.
⠀
■ BETWEEN THE FILE AND THE KERNEL
⠀
The YAML never reaches the kernel. netplan generate converts it into files for systemd-networkd on a server or NetworkManager on a desktop, and those back ends talk to the kernel. The generator runs again at every boot.
⠀
Building the same bond by hand, which is what one does when testing or mending, is a fiddly business with ip: nine commands, from ip link add bond0 type bond mode 802.3ad to ip link set vlan10 up. Their words appear nowhere in the YAML. The file says interfaces where the prompt says master, and even the shared word link means something else in each. Two vocabularies for one job, with a translator in the middle.
⠀
The translator also forgets. Its own manual says netplan apply "will not remove virtual devices such as bridges and bonds" that are no longer in the file, because "Netplan operates statelessly". Take the bond out of the YAML and it stays in the kernel until someone deletes it or reboots.
⠀
■ THE SAME JOB ON FREEBSD
⠀
cloned_interfaces="lagg0"
ifconfig_lagg0="laggproto lacp laggport em0 laggport em1 up"
vlans_lagg0="10"
ifconfig_lagg0_10="inet 192.0.2.10/24"
⠀
Four lines in /etc/rc.conf, straight from the Handbook. At boot rc.d/netif hands the quoted words to ifconfig, the same binary in the same base system. At the prompt it is two commands:
⠀
ifconfig lagg0 create laggproto lacp laggport em0 laggport em1 up
ifconfig lagg0.10 create vlan 10 vlandev lagg0 inet 192.0.2.10/24
⠀
One vocabulary, and nothing translates it. On a restart netif calls clone_down for what it created, so the machine ends up with exactly what rc.conf describes.
⠀
■ TRYING IT SAFELY
⠀
The real fear with remote network changes is losing the session, and with it the machine. Schedule shutdown -r +5 first, then build the bundle at the prompt with ifconfig, which changes the running system and leaves rc.conf alone. If the session dies, the machine reboots into what it had. If it survives, a kill to the pending shutdown calls the reboot off, and the very same words go into rc.conf, so the lines you keep are the lines you have just tested.
⠀
■ THE LIMIT
⠀
netplan try packages the rollback in a single step; on FreeBSD the safety net is one line typed before anything else. Namespaces and policy routing live in ip on Linux, and FreeBSD gives those jobs to the jail and the FIB, with ifconfig taking part through vnet and fib. Since 13.2 FreeBSD speaks netlink as well, so Linux tools can talk to it, while the native path stays ifconfig. And on a laptop that wanders between Wi-Fi networks NetworkManager earns its keep; a server's configuration is written once and read for years.
⠀
On FreeBSD the words you test at the prompt are the words you keep.
⠀

⚠️ 🇨🇦 🧠 Carney’s $1.6-Billion Cohere Stake Faces Reality Check as Models Rank Near 210th on Arena at 1354 Elo

Prime Minister Mark Carney’s claim that Canadians will own a piece of Cohere’s “world-leading secure AI” is marketing language that independent human-preference rankings have already disproven, with the firm’s strongest model at roughly 1354 Elo and near 210th overall.

On October 29, 2026, the federal government announced an equity investment of up to $1.6 billion in Toronto-based Cohere as part of a financing round targeting roughly $7 billion and a post-money valuation near $35.7 billion. The official release described the move as giving Canadians a stake in “secure, sovereign AI” built in Canada, with commitments that the company remain headquartered in the country and invest at least $1.7 billion in domestic computing infrastructure by 2030. Carney’s accompanying post on X repeated the “world-leading” framing.

The numbers on the LMSYS Chatbot Arena, the most widely cited blind human-preference ranking, tell a different story. As of late October 2026 snapshots, Cohere’s strongest listed model, Command A (03-2025), sits at approximately 1354 Elo. That places the lab around 23rd or 24th among roughly 28 providers and the model itself near 209th to 215th overall. Leading systems from Anthropic and Google routinely score above 1500, with gaps of 150 points or more that reflect clear differences in user preference on open-ended tasks.

Even within enterprise-focused or open-weight categories, Command A does not dominate. Aggregators show it lagging frontier proprietary models on agentic, coding, and knowledge work while remaining competitive mainly on cost or deployment constraints. Other Cohere variants rank still lower. By contrast, systems developed by xAI, including Grok variants, appear in the mid-to-high 1470s on the same Arena boards—materially closer to the current frontier without requiring a multi-billion-dollar government equity injection to declare national leadership.

Sovereign Super Intelligence capacity is a legitimate strategic objective. Data residency, controlled deployments, and reduced dependence on a handful of foreign providers matter for governments and regulated industries. Cohere has focused on private deployments and regulated sectors, which is a real commercial niche. That niche, however, is not the same as frontier capability. Equating a mid-tier provider with “world-leading” status requires the public to ignore the ranking data that every other serious lab tracks daily.

The investment also illustrates the recurring risk of industrial policy that picks winners with taxpayer capital. The round includes private participants such as Nvidia and Schwarz Group; the government’s stake is staged and commercial on paper. Yet the accompanying rhetoric treats the equity purchase as proof of technological sovereignty rather than a concentrated bet on one firm whose public benchmarks have not kept pace with the leaders. History in this sector shows that capability gaps are closed by research velocity and compute scale, not by press releases.

Canadians can reasonably want domestic Super Intelligence options that protect sensitive data and keep economic upside at home. Those goals are better served by accurate measurement of what the technology actually delivers than by promotional language that independent rankings contradict. The Arena numbers are public, updated, and based on millions of blind votes. They remain the clearest available check on claims of world leadership.

In September, we said that K2 Horizon was the largest LLM open drop in AI history yet. We’ve now delivered on the commitment.

When people say open models, they usually mean open weights. K2 Horizon 360 is way more: 8 artifact categories and 30+ repositories across every stage of LLM training.

- Checkpoints: 380 across the six models, pre-training through RL, so you can trace when a capability first appeared
- Data: 13 trillion pre-training tokens across 5 datasets and 24 subsets
- Data tools: 11 repositories, 7 task generation and 3 advanced generation pipelines
- New architecture: MoVA in our 36B-A4B model, MoE sparsity applied to the value vectors in multi-head attention, compatible with efficient attention algorithms at no additional KV-cache cost
- Pre-training infra: xLLM, faster pre-training and fine-tuning, with rework and reconfiguration at lower cost
- Post-training infra: RL360 for long-horizon agentic RL, 8192 concurrent sandboxes, 150 steps in 7 days, ~1.3M rollouts. It separates system crashes from the model’s own mistakes
- Training logs: 58 runs, with loss curves, gradient norms and the configs that actually ran, so you can check your own against a real one at this scale
- Diffusion LLM: Uno, autoregressive quality at diffusion speed

Voice AI is now good enough that preference and human-likeness can be scored as separate targets.

@voicearena_ai launched a new benchmark, Turing TTS to score the second one directly: listeners hear the same sentence from a person and from a model, then pick the person.

How often they pick the model is the Fool Rate. 50% would mean listeners can’t tell.

Even the best model, Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS, fooled them about 10% of the time.

On Voice Arena’s preference board, the top four models are statistically tied. Measured against a human, the whole field still has a long way to go.
